title: Research Into Child Psychology Is Largely the Study of Captivity Effects
author: Peter Gray
summary: Peter Gray argues, building on a new paper by Cevin Soling and Kathryn Burrows, that standard schools meet the scientific definition of captivity environments, and that most child psychology research is therefore conducted on 'captive' children rather than children behaving naturally. He contends this distorts our understanding of childhood by overrepresenting stress, helplessness, and academic behavior while underrepresenting curiosity, play, and cooperation -- traits better studied in free, unschooled, or Self-Directed Education settings.
points: Soling and Burrows define captivity by four criteria (movement constraint, segregation, institutional provision of needs, taming via control) and show ordinary schools meet all four.
Because captive subjects are easiest to study, most child psychology research is effectively research on captive children, not children in their natural state.
Animal captivity research shows anger, anxiety, depression, learned helplessness, and elevated stress hormones -- effects Gray says school-based research on children largely ignores.
Gray argues schooling produces 'taught helplessness' through reward/punishment systems that suppress children's initiative and creativity.
Curiosity and playfulness -- core traits of childhood -- are understudied because they are suppressed in school and can't be captured by the experimental paradigm.
Age-segregation and forced competition in school are described as artifacts of coercive schooling, not natural childhood behavior.
Gray recommends studying children in Self-Directed Education centers, hunter-gatherer societies, or unschooled cultures to see children's true biological nature.
quotes: Cevin is not one to mince words. He calls something what it is.

Soling and Burrows define captivity, just as researchers studying captive animals or humans in prison define it, as a condition that includes the following four components: (1) constraint on preferred movements, (2) segregation from attached environments, (3) institutional provision of survival needs, and (4) taming through privacy reduction and behavior control.

The experimental method is regarded as the queen of methods for studying cause-effect relationships. In experiments, you manipulate the conditions for different groups, or for the same group at different times, and record the behavioral effects.
the major lesson in school is obedience. To avoid punishment and pass in school, the main requirement is that you do what you are told to do, no matter how silly or stupid it is.
Reviews suggest that captivity has dramatic effects on moods: It can create anger, anxiety, and/or depression. It can create purposeless pacing or what might be called behavioral tics.
Soling and Burrows contend, quite aptly, that coercive schools are not just settings for learned helplessness; they are settings for taught helplessness.
Arguably (maybe inarguably) the most defining characteristics of childhood are curiosity and playfulness, yet relatively little can be found on these in the research literature on child psychology.

Another way, however, is to think of the purpose as that of understanding children as biological creations of Mother Nature (natural selection), who innately strive to take control of their lives, strive for independence, and play and explore in quite remarkable ways when free to do so.
